# Sarabhamigajātaka (Ja 483)

**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sarabhamigajātaka* (Ja 483) is a birth story belonging to the *Terasanipāta* (Thirteen Nipāta) of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1887; SuttaCentral]. Its opening verse commences with *Āsimseth’ eva puriso* ("Toil on, O man") [Fausböll 1887; SuttaCentral]. In the narrative of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta is born as a stag (*sarabhamiga*) who, displaying compassion and virtue, rescues a hunter who had previously pursued him [Spink 2007; Fausböll 1887]. In the conclusion of the story (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the characters from that former life: the king was Ānanda, the chaplain was Sāriputta, and the stag was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1887].
The text is especially celebrated for its extensive introductory story of the present (*paccupannavatthu*). Framed by the Buddha delivering a succinct query that Sāriputta explains in full [Fausböll 1887; SuttaCentral], it discusses the distinct spiritual capacities of the chief disciples [Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. It incorporates an elaborate account of the Great Miracle at Sāvatthī (Śrāvastī), the Buddha's ascent to the Tāvatiṃsa (Trayastriṃśa) heaven to preach the Abhidhamma to the deities for three months, and his dramatic descent to earth (*devāvatāra* / *devorohana*) at Saṅkassa (Sāṅkāśya) upon a triple stairway of gold, jewels, and silver, escorted by Śakra and Brahmā [Glasenapp 1966; Anderson 1978; Waldschmidt 1971; Shulman n.d.]. Both the stag narrative and this introductory descent sequence are prominent subjects in early Buddhist art and sculpture, including reliefs at Bharhut and Sanchi, paintings at Ajanta, and Gandharan sculptural representations [Anderson 1978; Spink 2007; Ali and Qazi 2008].
SuttaCentral lists passage-level parallels with the *Mahāsīlavajātaka* (Ja 51) and the *Mahājanakajātaka* (Ja 539) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates extensive text reuse, matching segments §1.1–6.4 of Ja 483 with §13.6–19.4 of *Mahājanakajātaka* with identical wording, in addition to matches across the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Ekakanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the *Kavidappaṇanīti* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also records machine-generated cross-language alignments between Ja 483 and the Tibetan translation of Haribhaṭṭa's *Jātakamālā* (*haribhaṭṭajātakamālā-nāma*, D4152) [DharmaNexus].
